description: When love hurts, obsesses, disappoints, or refuses to let go — four poems on complicated love.
content_html:
Love That Refuses to Be Simple

Not all love is joyful or straightforward. Some of the most powerful poems in the OCR anthology explore the darker, more complicated dimensions of love: grief that will not release its grip, obsession that traps the speaker, disappointment when love fails to appear, and desire entangled with anger and heartbreak. These poems resist the comfortable idealism of romantic tradition and instead confront the messiness of real feeling.

The four poems studied in this lesson each present a different variety of complicated love: Tony Harrison’s grief that outlasts death, Jackie Kay’s obsession with a phone call that never comes, Thomas Hardy’s quiet devastation at an unfulfilled appointment, and James Fenton’s wry mixture of anger and new desire after a broken heart. Together they reveal that love is rarely clean or resolved.

Key Fact

The four poems in this lesson each explore a different strand of complicated love: Harrison’s “Long Distance II” (grief and denial), Kay’s “Dusting the Phone” (obsessive waiting), Hardy’s “A Broken Appointment” (disappointed expectation), and Fenton’s “In Paris With You” (post-heartbreak desire).

“Long Distance II” — Tony Harrison

Harrison’s poem begins with a striking detail: though his mother was already two years dead, his father “kept her slippers warming by the gas” and “still went to renew her transport pass.” These small, domestic acts of denial are not signs of madness but of overwhelming love — a love so deep that death cannot yet undo the habits of a shared life. The father performs rituals of care even for someone no longer there to receive them.

The speaker initially distances himself from his father’s grief: the father hides it, “to clear away her things and look alone / as though his still raw love were such a crime.” The confessional turn comes in the final stanza, where Harrison admits he rationally believes “life ends with death, and that is all” — but then reveals that in his own phone book he has kept “the disconnected number I still call.” The poem ends by implicating the speaker in the very same denial he observed in his father.

The word “disconnected” works on two levels: the phone line is literally cut off, and so is the human connection it represented. Yet Harrison “still” calls — the adverb carrying enormous weight. The rational voice of the third stanza (“I believe life ends with death”) is completely undercut by this act. The volta in the final stanza shifts the poem from a portrait of his father to a confession about himself. Love, Harrison suggests, persists even when we tell ourselves it should not.

Key Fact

Harrison uses the sonnet form — traditionally associated with love poetry — to contain grief. The poem’s final volta (“You haven’t both gone shopping; just the same”) is a pivot from the father’s story to the speaker’s own admission, structurally mimicking the way grief unexpectedly catches us.

“Dusting the Phone” — Jackie Kay

Kay’s poem is a study in the torment of obsessive waiting. The speaker “assault[s] the postman for a letter” and “dress[es] for” the phone, polishing it until it shines: “Silver service. I polish it. I dress for it. / I’ll give it extra in return for your call.” The personification of the phone as something that can be bribed or pleased is both darkly comic and painfully accurate — when we are desperate to hear from someone, we behave irrationally, projecting feeling onto objects.

The poem’s imagery builds dread. “The future is a long gloved hand. An empty cup.” The fragmented syntax — short, blunt noun phrases — mirrors the speaker’s fractured mental state. The phone “sends me hoaxes, wrong numbers” and the beloved’s “voice / disappears into my lonely cotton sheets.” The desperation escalates until the poem breaks down into a direct, raw appeal: “Come on, damn you, ring me. Or else. What? / I don’t know what.” The trailing, unresolved ending enacts the speaker’s powerlessness.

Kay uses a second-person address (“You say, don’t mention love”) that implicates the absent beloved without ever describing them. The “you” remains entirely mysterious — we know nothing about this person except the power they hold over the speaker. The present-tense narration (“This very second I am waiting on the phone”) traps the reader in the same moment of tension the speaker cannot escape. This creates one of the poem’s most distinctive effects: time seems to stop, as it does when we are waiting for something we desperately want.

“A Broken Appointment” — Thomas Hardy

Hardy’s poem opens with a devastating simplicity: “You did not come.” Four words. The short first sentence is followed by the slow, measured weight of time passing: “And marching Time drew on, and wore me numb.” Hardy chooses “numb” precisely — his grief is not hot and weeping but cold and hollow, as if the feeling has been worn away by waiting.

What distinguishes this poem from simple disappointment is Hardy’s analysis of why the missed appointment hurts. He explicitly states he grieves “yet less for loss of your dear presence there / Than that I thus found lacking in your make / That high compassion which can overbear / Reluctance for pure lovingkindness’ sake.” In other words: he does not simply miss her — he grieves the discovery that she lacks the human compassion to come even as a lovingkindness, not a declaration of love. The repetition of “You did not come” and “You love not me” at the start and end of each stanza creates a formal, tolling echo of loss.

“In Paris With You” — James Fenton

Fenton’s poem is ostensibly about a romantic trip to Paris, but the speaker refuses romance from the very first line: “Don’t talk to me of love. I’ve had an earful.” He is “one of your talking wounded” — bruised by a recent relationship (“angry at the way I’ve been bamboozled”) and explicitly “on the rebound.” His wry self-awareness (“I admit I’m on the rebound”) is the poem’s most interesting quality: he knows exactly what he is doing and does it anyway.

The poem plays with tourist clichés. Instead of the Louvre, the Champs-Élysées, Notre-Dame, he wants to stay in “this sleazy / Old hotel room.” The rhyme scheme is deliberately comic — “bamboozled” and “maroonded” are almost nonsense rhymes that deflate the grandeur of Paris and of love itself. Yet the poem ends with genuine tenderness: “I’m in Paris with your eyes, your mouth, / I’m in Paris with… all points south.” The aposiopesis (“… all points south”) combines desire and embarrassment, suggesting that real feeling has broken through the defensive humour.

Grief and denial (Harrison): Love here outlasts the beloved’s life. Harrison and his father are both trapped by affection that reason cannot dissolve. The complication is the gap between what the speaker believes intellectually and what he does emotionally.

Obsessive waiting (Kay): Love here is destabilising and imprisoning. The speaker acknowledges “I am spending my time imagining the worst that could happen” and knows it is irrational, yet cannot stop. The complication is that love and anxiety have become indistinguishable.

Failed compassion (Hardy): Love here is one-sided and quietly devastating. The complication is not just that she did not come, but that the speaker has now seen clearly that she lacks the capacity for compassionate love he hoped for.

Post-heartbreak desire (Fenton): Love here is entangled with self-knowledge and defensive irony. The complication is the speaker’s simultaneous refusal of love and surrender to it — he says “don’t talk to me of love” while clearly falling for someone new.
exam_tip_html: In comparison questions on this collection, examiners reward students who can discuss the complexity of emotion rather than labelling it simply as “sad” or “happy.” When writing about these four poems, name the specific complication: Harrison’s rational disbelief vs. emotional behaviour, Kay’s obsession that she recognises but cannot escape, Hardy’s focus on compassion rather than reciprocated feeling, and Fenton’s ironic self-awareness. For AO3, consider how poets across different periods and genders handle the same theme differently — this is exactly what OCR’s comparison task rewards.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Harrison’s “Long Distance II” shows grief as a form of love that outlasts death, ending with a personal confession: “the disconnected number I still call.”
  • Kay’s “Dusting the Phone” presents obsessive, anxious waiting as love, where the speaker acknowledges her own irrationality but cannot escape it.
  • Hardy’s “A Broken Appointment” grieves the discovery that the woman lacks basic compassion, not just the absence of romantic love. Fenton’s “In Paris With You” uses wry humour and deflated tourist clichés to show desire breaking through defensive cynicism after heartbreak.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how Harrison uses the contrast between his father's behaviour and his own stated beliefs to present grief in 'Long Distance II'. Refer to: 'I believe life ends with death, and that is all' and 'the disconnected number I still call'.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Perceptive analysis of the contradiction between the rational declaration ('I believe life ends with death') and the emotional act of calling a disconnected number. Explores how the volta in the final stanza shifts the poem from portrait of the father to confession about the speaker. May discuss the word 'still' as carrying the poem's emotional weight, or the sonnet form as a vehicle traditionally associated with love. Precise use of terminology throughout.
Secure: Clear analysis of the contrast with relevant quotations and appropriate terminology.
Developing: Some understanding of the contradiction with basic comment on effect.
Emerging: Simple paraphrase of events with limited analysis.

practice_questions.text: How does Jackie Kay use imagery and form to present obsessive love in 'Dusting the Phone'? Refer to specific details from the poem.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Explores the personification of the phone ('I polish it. I dress for it') as a displaced focus for longing. Analyses how fragmented syntax and short declarative sentences mirror the speaker's fractured mental state. Discusses the unresolved ending ('I don't know what') as structurally enacting powerlessness. May link to the speaker's self-awareness ('I know this is not a good idea') as a complicating layer of understanding without resolution.
Secure: Clear analysis of personification and/or fragmented form with relevant quotations.
Developing: Some comment on imagery or tone with basic explanation.
Emerging: Simple description of events or feelings with minimal textual reference.

practice_questions.text: Compare how failed or one-sided love is presented in 'A Broken Appointment' and one other poem from the Love and Relationships collection. [40 marks]
practice_questions.marks:
AO1 (up to 15 marks): Compares how each poem presents love that is not returned or fulfilled. Hardy: quiet devastation at absent compassion, not just absent love; the discovery that the woman lacks 'high compassion'. Comparison poem: student's choice with sustained thematic link. Comparison maintained throughout.
AO2 (up to 15 marks): Analyses methods in both poems. Hardy: repetition of 'You did not come' / 'You love not me', the tolling formal structure of two-stanza ballade-like form, lexical field of time ('marching Time', 'wore me numb'). Comparison poem: relevant technique analysis with terminology.
AO3 (up to 10 marks): Context relevant to both poems — Victorian attitudes to social obligation, the expectation of compassion in relationships, gender and power dynamics.

practice_questions.text: Explore how Fenton uses humour and informal language to present complicated desire in 'In Paris With You'. Refer to: 'Don't talk to me of love. I've had an earful' and 'I'm in Paris with your eyes, your mouth'.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analyses the tension between the dismissive opening ('Don't talk to me of love') and the genuine tenderness of the closing lines. Explores deliberate comic rhymes ('bamboozled'/'maroonded') as a form of emotional self-defence. Discusses how the repeated refrain ('I'm in Paris with you') shifts from defiance to affection. May note the aposiopesis ('... all points south') as desire breaking through irony.
Secure: Clear analysis of the humour and its relationship to genuine feeling with relevant references.
Developing: Some comment on the informal tone or the contradiction with basic explanation.
Emerging: Simple description of the speaker's attitude with limited textual support.

practice_questions.text: How does Harrison present the relationship between love and rational thought in 'Long Distance II'?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Explores how the poem sets up rational belief ('I believe life ends with death, and that is all') only to undercut it with emotional behaviour (calling a disconnected number). Analyses the father's rituals — warming slippers, renewing transport pass — as irrational but deeply loving acts. Discusses the word 'still' in the final line as signalling love's persistence beyond reason. May discuss the sonnet's volta as the structural moment where reason gives way.
Secure: Clear analysis of the contrast between reason and emotion with relevant quotations.
Developing: Some awareness of the contradiction with basic comment.
Emerging: Paraphrase with limited analysis.

practice_questions.text: Compare how poets present the emotional experience of waiting or absence in 'Dusting the Phone' and one other poem from the Love and Relationships collection. [40 marks]
practice_questions.marks:
AO1 (up to 15 marks): Compares how absence or waiting creates emotional suffering. Kay: obsessive waiting for a phone call; time stops; anxiety and love become indistinguishable. Comparison poem: relevant presentation of absence, distance, or waiting. Sustained comparison.
AO2 (up to 15 marks): Analyses methods. Kay: personification of the phone, fragmented syntax, present tense, second-person address, unresolved ending. Comparison poem: relevant technique analysis.
AO3 (up to 10 marks): Context relevant to both poems — modern technology and love, the vulnerability of emotional dependency, the relationship between communication and connection.

knowledge_checks.q: In 'Long Distance II', what does Harrison admit to doing at the end of the poem despite believing 'life ends with death'?
options: Keeping his mother's letters in a drawer
Still calling a disconnected phone number
Leaving her slippers warming by the fire

knowledge_checks.q: In 'A Broken Appointment', why does Hardy say he grieves most deeply when the woman does not come?
options: Because he is in love with her and she rejected him
Because she has shown she lacks basic human compassion
Because he had waited in the rain all afternoon
Because she promised to bring him important news

knowledge_checks.q: In 'Dusting the Phone', Kay writes that she is spending her time imagining the _____ that could happen, knowing this is not a good idea.
Fenton describes himself in 'In Paris With You' as 'one of your talking _____', using the phrase to suggest he is emotionally wounded.
Match each poem to its central complication of love:

flashcard_questions.q: What does 'the disconnected number I still call' reveal about Harrison in 'Long Distance II'?
flashcard_questions.a: He calls his dead parents' number despite believing life ends with death — grief persists beyond rational belief.

flashcard_questions.q: What does Harrison's father do to keep his dead wife present in 'Long Distance II'?
flashcard_questions.a: Kept her slippers warming by the gas and still went to renew her transport pass.

flashcard_questions.q: What poetic form does Harrison use in 'Long Distance II', and why is it significant?
flashcard_questions.a: A sonnet — traditionally a love poem form, used here to contain grief and loss instead.

flashcard_questions.q: Why does the speaker in 'Dusting the Phone' polish and dress for the phone?
flashcard_questions.a: She personifies the phone as something that can be appeased or rewarded into bringing a call from her beloved.

flashcard_questions.q: How does Kay end 'Dusting the Phone', and what does this suggest?
flashcard_questions.a: 'I don't know what' — the unresolved ending enacts the speaker's powerlessness and emotional paralysis.

flashcard_questions.q: In 'A Broken Appointment', what does Hardy say he grieves more than the woman's absence?
flashcard_questions.a: That she lacks 'high compassion' — the discovery she cannot perform basic lovingkindness.

flashcard_questions.q: What phrase does Hardy repeat to create a tolling echo of loss in 'A Broken Appointment'?
flashcard_questions.a: 'You did not come' (stanza 1) and 'You love not me' (stanza 2) — repeated at the start and close of each stanza.

flashcard_questions.q: What does 'Don't talk to me of love. I've had an earful' tell us about the speaker in 'In Paris With You'?
flashcard_questions.a: He is recently heartbroken and defensive about love — but the poem reveals he is already falling for someone new.

flashcard_questions.q: What effect do Fenton's nonsense rhymes (e.g. 'bamboozled' / 'maroonded') create in 'In Paris With You'?
flashcard_questions.a: Comic deflation — the ludicrous rhymes undercut romantic grandeur and signal the speaker's defensive irony.

flashcard_questions.q: What does Fenton mean by 'I'm in Paris with your eyes, your mouth'?
flashcard_questions.a: Despite rejecting romantic love at the start, the speaker is entirely absorbed in the new person's physical presence.

flashcard_questions.q: In 'Dusting the Phone', what does 'The future is a long gloved hand. An empty cup.' suggest?
flashcard_questions.a: The future feels alien, unreachable, and hollow — fragmented syntax mirrors the speaker's fractured anxiety.

flashcard_questions.q: What does the word 'still' do in the final line of 'Long Distance II'?
flashcard_questions.a: It carries the poem's emotional weight — showing grief's persistence despite the rational declaration that death is final.

glossary_terms.definition: Love that is painful, obsessive, one-sided, or fraught with grief, ambivalence, or disappointment rather than simple joy.
Refusing to accept a painful reality, often unconsciously, as a way of managing grief or loss.
A mode of poetry in which the speaker shares deeply personal experience, often admitting difficult truths about themselves.
A turning point in a poem where the argument, tone, or perspective shifts — especially common in sonnets.
A fourteen-line poem, often in iambic pentameter, traditionally exploring love or a single idea with a structural turn near the end.
Giving human qualities or agency to an object, animal, or abstract idea.
A poetic voice that addresses a 'you', creating immediacy and intimacy while keeping the addressed person mysterious.
A kind act performed not from romantic love but from basic human decency and compassionate care for another person.
A tone that combines humour and seriousness, often using self-mockery to deflect from genuine or painful feeling.
A figure of speech in which a sentence is deliberately left incomplete, often for comic, ironic, or emotional effect.
